title: Disorders of hemostasis
covers: Case-based review of platelet disorders (thrombocytopenia, ITP, HIT, DIC, TTP, HUS, inherited platelet function disorders), coagulation disorders (vitamin K deficiency, factor XIII deficiency, liver disease), von Willebrand disease, vessel wall disorders, and bedside clues to the diagnosis.

items.p: Epistaxis in children is mostly local (upper respiratory infection, allergy), but it can be a bleeding disorder.
Red flags: epistaxis lasting > 30 minutes, recurrent or severe enough to need red cell transfusions; severe anemia.
Suspect a severe bleeding disorder with: early onset, prolonged, recurrent or postoperative bleeding, need for transfusions, positive family history.
Inherited disorders: infancy and early childhood, bleeding in males (X-linked, e.g. hemophilia), past postoperative bleeding, positive family history.

table: Male toddler, deep tissue or joint bleeding
Girl with heavy periods and mucocutaneous bleeding
Well, one bleeding site (e.g. one nostril)

items.p: Platelets: 2–3 µm, non-nucleated fragments of megakaryocytes; production regulated by thrombopoietin; normal count 150–450 × 10⁹/L.
Defects are acquired or inherited, of number (thrombocytopenia; thrombocytosis, reactive or primary) or function (receptors: Bernard–Soulier, Glanzmann; release/storage; biochemical pathways).

table: Marrow failure (aplastic anemia, MDS, myelofibrosis, leukemia), megaloblastic anemia, infections, drugs (chemotherapy, ethanol, sulfas), radiotherapy
Cirrhosis with portal hypertension, splenic tumor, sickle cell disease. 30% of platelets sit in a normal spleen, 90% in an enlarged one; often with anemia or leukopenia

items.note: Slide 5 gives a platelet life span of 5–7 days; most references give about 7–10 days. Not tested.

items.p: The most common acquired autoimmune bleeding disorder of childhood. Isolated thrombocytopenia (< 100 × 10⁹/L) with no other cause: a diagnosis of exclusion.

ul: Peaks at 2–5 years; more cases in spring and early summer
About 80% primary; secondary with SLE, APS, CVID, CLL, Evans, ALPS, HIV, hepatitis C, H. pylori, vaccines, infection
Mechanism: increased destruction (autoantibodies, macrophage phagocytosis, cytotoxic T cells) and decreased production (impaired megakaryocyte maturation)
Course: ~70% resolve within 6 months; chronic (> 12 months) in 20–30% of children
Presentation: sudden mucocutaneous bleeding in a well child (petechiae, purpura, gums, nose, GI, hematuria, heavy periods); intracranial hemorrhage very rare; fatigue in 22%
Case: platelets 4,000/mm³, high MPV, large platelets = young platelets → increased destruction (lecturer's notes)

items.p: Severe = clinically significant bleeding requiring treatment. Refractory = significant thrombocytopenia and/or bleeding despite first- and second-line therapies.

Reconsider ITP with: recurrent infections and eczema, bone pain, constitutional symptoms, family history, dysmorphic features, organomegaly, marked lymphadenopathy or masses, anemia or neutropenia, blasts. A normal exam with isolated thrombocytopenia supports ITP.

items.note: Slide 18 says "most children are asymptomatic"; most references describe mild mucocutaneous bleeding as the usual presentation. Not tested.

ul: Goal: a platelet count with adequate hemostasis, not a normal count
Decide on bleeding severity (not the count alone), preference, quality of life and durable response
Traditional: observation, steroids, IVIG, anti-D immunoglobulin, splenectomy
Novel: rituximab (anti-CD20), thrombopoietin receptor agonists
2019 paradigm: observe mild ITP → short steroids when treatment is needed → TPO-RA if first line fails
An immune reaction 5–15 days after heparin
IgG binds the platelet factor 4–heparin complex and platelets → platelet activation, thrombocytopenia, more thrombin
Result: thrombosis (DVT, PE, cerebral venous sinus, limb, stroke, MI)
Treatment: stop heparin and give a non-heparin anticoagulant

items.note: Slide 21 says HIT leads to "bleeding and thrombosis"; standard sources stress thrombosis, with bleeding uncommon despite the low count. Only thrombosis is tested.

items.p: Schistocytes + thrombocytopenia = thrombotic microangiopathy until proven otherwise.

table: Sepsis, trauma, cancer, obstetric, transfusion reaction
Anti-ADAMTS13 antibody, or ADAMTS13 gene variants
Shiga toxin (STEC, Shigella), or complement dysregulation (atypical)

items.p: DIC: coagulation and fibrinolysis activated inside vessels → thrombosis, bleeding, organ damage. Fever, profuse bleeding, shock, multi-organ failure, purpura fulminans. Labs: low platelets, prolonged PT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, schistocytes. Treat the cause; platelets, plasma or cryoprecipitate (fibrinogen-rich) for bleeding.
TTP: rare; ADAMTS13 normally cleaves large vWF multimers. Treatment: supportive, plasmapheresis (removes anti-ADAMTS13 antibodies), immunosuppressants, ADAMTS13 replacement.
HUS: MAHA + thrombocytopenia + acute kidney injury; 90% after Shiga toxin-producing E. coli or Shigella dysenteriae; typically children; clinical diagnosis; supportive care.

Rare bleeding disorders with mucocutaneous bleeding and usually a normal count. Mostly acquired: aspirin, NSAIDs, penicillin, cephalosporins, anticonvulsants; uremia, liver disease, autoimmune disease. Inherited forms are mostly AR with early-onset bleeding.
All three are AR; GT and BSS occur in about 1 in 1 million. Among rare bleeding disorders, factor VII deficiency is reported most often.
Diagnosis: early-onset bleeding, family history, normal PT and aPTT, abnormal platelet function studies, absent glycoproteins on flow cytometry, genetic testing in selected cases.
Treatment by bleeding severity: platelet transfusion; recombinant factor VIIa if platelet-refractory.
Case: a man with lifelong transfusion-dependent nosebleeds, normal platelet count and size, normal PT and aPTT → Glanzmann thrombasthenia (worked out; the slides give no answer).
Inherited: hemophilia (separate lecture), other factor deficiencies. Acquired: warfarin, heparin, chemotherapy; vitamin K deficiency; DIC; inhibitors; liver disease.

ul: Hemophilia case: a 15-month-old boy, swollen knee and forehead hematoma, bleeding maternal uncle, normal CBC and PT, prolonged aPTT
Factor XIII deficiency case: bleeding after tonsillectomy, delayed umbilical cord bleeding, poor wound healing, miscarriages, consanguinity; platelets, PT, aPTT, thrombin time and smear all normal

items.p: Vitamin K deficiency:

ul: Vitamin K (fat soluble; leafy vegetables, colonic bacteria) is needed for II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S
Causes: low intake (breast milk), poor absorption (celiac disease, cystic fibrosis), newborns, prolonged antibiotics, warfarin
Most common in newborns (hemorrhagic disease of the newborn); late form up to 3 months
PT prolonged first (isolated early), then PTT; treat with vitamin K and the cause

items.note: Slide 37 places intracranial and retroperitoneal bleeding in the "early form, 1–7 days". Most references split it into early (< 24 h), classic (2–7 days, GI, skin, umbilical) and late (2–12 weeks, often intracranial). Timings and sites are not tested.

items.p: Liver cirrhosis:

ul: Lower synthesis of most factors except VIII; portal hypertension → big spleen traps platelets
Bilirubin up, albumin down, PT and aPTT prolonged
Fresh frozen plasma (all clotting factors) for active bleeding
Vitamin K corrects the PT in vitamin K deficiency, not in liver failure. A low factor V points to liver failure (V is not vitamin K dependent).

items.note: The slide 45 figure lists "↓ AST and ALT" in late cirrhosis; transaminases are usually normal or mildly raised then rather than low. Not tested.

items.p: The most common congenital bleeding disorder (~1%, males and females equally). A quantitative or qualitative vWF defect → poor platelet adhesion and a secondary coagulation defect. Mostly asymptomatic; found through family history or preoperative screening. Mucocutaneous bleeding (joints in type 3), prolonged bleeding time and aPTT.
Think of vWD in every adolescent girl with heavy periods, iron deficiency and no gynecologic cause.
Case: a 14-year-old girl with heavy periods, nosebleeds, a hemarthrosis, an aunt with an early hysterectomy, normal platelets and PT, prolonged aPTT that corrects on mixing.

table: Marked lack of vWF and FVIII; hemophilia-like
Loss of high-molecular-weight multimers, low activity
vWF binds GPIb too avidly; sometimes thrombocytopenia
Poor vWF binding to FVIII; low FVIII, normal vWF activity; suspect in females with isolated FVIII deficiency

items.p: Treatment:

ul: Desmopressin (DDAVP) for type 1 and most type 2: endothelial release of vWF, vWF/FVIII up 2–5-fold
vWF replacement for non-responders and severe cases
Antifibrinolytics for mucosal bleeding; platelet transfusion in type 2B
Bypassing agents (rFVIIa, PCC) in severe cases and with inhibitors to infused vWF
Supportive: no contact sports, aspirin or NSAIDs; estrogen or endometrial ablation for heavy periods

items.note: The backup table (slide 52) lists DDAVP for type 2B. Standard guidance usually avoids DDAVP in 2B because it can worsen thrombocytopenia. Not tested; ask the lecturer.

summary.h: When the vessel is the problem

table: Purpura on buttocks and legs, arthritis, abdominal pain, nephritis; commonest childhood vasculitis
Normal platelets and clotting; check urine
Perifollicular bleeding, corkscrew hairs, swollen bleeding gums
Diet history; response to vitamin C
Stretchy skin, hypermobile joints, bruising, poor wound healing
Recurrent epistaxis, telangiectasia on lips and fingers, AVMs in lung, liver, brain
Flat purple patches on forearms and hands

items.p: Coagulation occurs on the surfaces of platelets and endothelial cells.

cards.a: > 30 minutes, recurrent, needs red cell transfusion; severe anemia
Decreased production, increased destruction (immune or nonimmune), splenic sequestration

cards.q: Share of platelets in a normal versus an enlarged spleen
cards.a: About 30% versus 90%
DIC, TTP, HUS
Isolated thrombocytopenia < 100 × 10⁹/L with no other cause; a diagnosis of exclusion
~70% resolve within 6 months; chronic (> 12 months) in 20–30%
Newly diagnosed 0–3 months; persistent 3–12 months; chronic ≥ 12 months
Increased destruction (antibodies, macrophages, cytotoxic T cells) and impaired megakaryocyte maturation
Infections with eczema, bone pain, constitutional symptoms, organomegaly, lymphadenopathy, anemia or neutropenia, blasts
Observe mild ITP → short steroids → TPO receptor agonist
IgG against PF4–heparin activates platelets → thrombosis; stop heparin, give a non-heparin anticoagulant
Low platelets, prolonged PT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, schistocytes

cards.q: DIC versus TTP versus HUS: key separators
cards.a: DIC: prolonged PT/aPTT. TTP: ADAMTS13 < 10%, brain and heart. HUS: Shiga toxin, kidney injury.
Plasmapheresis, immunosuppressants, ADAMTS13 replacement, supportive care
MAHA, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury; 90% after Shiga toxin (EHEC, Shigella)
AR; absent GPIIb/IIIa; normal count and size; aggregates with ristocetin only
AR; absent GPIb/IX/V; low count, large platelets; no aggregation with ristocetin
AR; no alpha granules; large gray platelets, low count; myelofibrosis, splenomegaly
Aspirin, NSAIDs, penicillin, cephalosporins, anticonvulsants; uremia, liver disease, autoimmune disease
Delayed umbilical cord bleeding, poor wound healing, miscarriages; all screening tests normal
Factors II, VII, IX, X; proteins C and S
Breast milk, malabsorption (celiac, CF), newborns, prolonged antibiotics, warfarin

cards.q: Liver failure versus vitamin K deficiency
cards.a: Vitamin K corrects the PT only in deficiency; low factor V points to liver failure
Factor VIII
~1%, most common congenital bleeding disorder; adolescent girl with heavy periods and iron deficiency
1: mild deficiency (70–80%, AD). 2: qualitative (15–20%). 3: marked vWF + FVIII deficiency (AR).
2B: vWF binds GPIb too avidly, low platelets. 2N: poor binding to FVIII, low FVIII.
Types 1 and most 2; releases endothelial vWF, raises vWF/FVIII 2–5-fold

cards.q: Vessel disorders: HSP, scurvy, EDS, HHT, senile purpura
cards.a: Immune complexes; vitamin C/collagen; inherited collagen; abnormal vessels; connective tissue loss

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl has had a nosebleed for an hour. Which feature is a red flag for a bleeding disorder?
questions.explanation: Red flags: long-lasting (> 30 minutes), recurrent, severe epistaxis needing red cell transfusions, and severe anemia. A: Points to a local cause. B: A common local cause. C: A common local cause. D: Reassuring.

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of nosebleeds in children?
questions.explanation: Epistaxis is common in children and mostly due to local conditions such as upper respiratory infections and allergy, but it can be due to a bleeding disorder. A: Possible, but less common. C: Possible, but less common. D: Rare. E: Rare.

questions.stem: Which hormone regulates the differentiation and proliferation of platelet precursors?
questions.explanation: Platelets are small (2–3 µm), non-nucleated fragments of megakaryocytes; their production is regulated by thrombopoietin. B: Red cells. C: Neutrophils. D: Eosinophils. E: Lymphocytes.

questions.stem: A child has a platelet count of 900 × 10⁹/L during recovery from pneumonia. How is this classified?
questions.explanation: Platelet number problems: thrombocytopenia (decreased production, increased destruction, splenic sequestration) and thrombocytosis (reactive or primary). A: A marrow disorder, not a response to illness. B: Lowers the count. D: Not a number problem. E: A function problem.

questions.stem: Bernard–Soulier syndrome and Glanzmann thrombasthenia are which kind of platelet defect?
questions.explanation: Function defects: receptors (Bernard–Soulier, Glanzmann), release/storage, biochemical pathways. A: E.g. gray platelet syndrome. B: Another function group. C: A number problem. E: A number problem.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old has macrocytic anemia, neutropenia and a platelet count of 40 × 10⁹/L. The marrow shows dysplasia. What is the mechanism of his thrombocytopenia?
questions.explanation: MDS: a clonal stem cell disorder with ineffective hematopoiesis, marrow dysplasia and cytopenias, with a risk of AML. It lowers platelets by decreased production. A: Not suggested by dysplasia. B: No splenomegaly given. C: Not suggested. D: Not suggested.

questions.stem: Each causes thrombocytopenia by decreased marrow production EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Decreased production: marrow failure, megaloblastic anemia, infections, drugs (chemotherapy, ethanol, sulfas), radiotherapy. Cirrhosis lowers platelets by splenic sequestration. A: Decreased production. C: Decreased production. D: Decreased production. E: Decreased production.

questions.stem: A man with cirrhosis has a large spleen, platelets of 60 × 10⁹/L and mild leukopenia. About what share of his platelets may be held in the spleen?
questions.explanation: About 30% of platelets are sequestered in the spleen normally and 90% with splenic enlargement; anemia and/or leukopenia often accompany it. A: The normal share. B: Below the share given for enlargement. D: Too low. E: Below the share given for enlargement.

questions.stem: Which disorder lowers the platelet count by splenic sequestration?
questions.explanation: Splenic sequestration: cirrhosis with portal hypertension and splenomegaly, splenic tumor, splenic malfunction in sickle cell disease. B: Decreased production. C: Immune destruction. D: Nonimmune destruction. E: Decreased production.

questions.stem: A healthy 18-year-old has sudden oral bleeding and petechiae, no organomegaly, platelets of 4,000/mm³, normal Hb and WBC, a high MPV and large platelets on the smear. What is the mechanism?
questions.explanation: Lecturer's notes: immune thrombocytopenia; large platelets = young platelets. The marrow is producing, so the platelets are being destroyed. A: Large young platelets show an active marrow. B: No splenomegaly. C: Not the cause. E: Not the cause.

questions.stem: A girl with immune thrombocytopenia has large platelets on her smear. What do they indicate?

options.C: Clumping of platelets in the tube
options.D: Old platelets pooled in the spleen
options.E: Young platelets from an active marrow

questions.explanation: Lecturer's notes: in ITP the platelet count falls and platelet size rises; large platelets are young platelets. A: Gray platelet syndrome. B: Bernard–Soulier syndrome. C: An artefact, not size. D: Not the explanation.

questions.stem: Which cause of increased platelet destruction is nonimmune?
questions.explanation: Immune: ITP, HIT, SLE. Nonimmune: DIC (a mixed platelet and coagulation disorder), TTP, HUS. B: Immune. C: Immune. D: Immune complexes. E: Immune.

questions.stem: Immune thrombocytopenia is defined by an isolated platelet count below what level?
questions.explanation: ITP: isolated thrombocytopenia (< 100 × 10⁹/L) without other causes; a diagnosis of exclusion. A: The lower limit of normal. B: Too low. D: Too low. E: Too low.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old has petechiae and a platelet count of 12 × 10⁹/L. How is ITP diagnosed?
questions.explanation: ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion: isolated thrombocytopenia in the absence of other causes or associated disorders. A: Not the basis of diagnosis. C: Not routinely. D: Used for function disorders. E: Used for inherited disorders.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old has just been diagnosed with ITP. About what is the chance of spontaneous resolution within 6 months?
questions.explanation: Childhood ITP is mostly self-limited, with ~70% spontaneous resolution in 6 months; chronic ITP (> 12 months) in 20–30%. A: Too low. B: Too low. C: Too high. E: Too low.

questions.stem: About what share of children with ITP develop chronic ITP?
questions.explanation: Chronic ITP (lasting > 12 months) is seen in 20–30% of children. B: Too low. C: Too low. D: Too high. E: The share that resolves.

questions.stem: At what age does childhood ITP peak?
questions.explanation: Childhood ITP incidence is highest at about 2–5 years and falls after that. A: Lower than the peak. B: After the peak. C: After the peak. D: Lowest.

questions.stem: Childhood ITP shows seasonal variability. When are cases most frequent?
questions.explanation: Monthly cases peak from about March to July and are lowest around October. A: The lowest months. B: Not the peak. D: Falling to the lowest point. E: Before the peak.

questions.stem: A child's ITP was diagnosed 5 months ago. How is it classified now?
questions.explanation: New classification: newly diagnosed 0–3 months, persistent 3–12 months, chronic ≥ 12 months. A: 0–3 months. C: 12 months or more. D: Needs failure of first- and second-line therapy. E: Needs clinically significant bleeding requiring treatment.

questions.stem: Which term describes ITP with clinically significant bleeding despite first- and second-line therapies?
questions.explanation: Refractory: persistent clinically significant thrombocytopenia and/or bleeding despite first- and second-line therapies, requiring treatment. Severe: clinically significant bleeding requiring treatment. A: Bleeding requiring treatment, not failed therapy. B: Duration ≥ 12 months. C: Duration 3–12 months. E: Duration 0–3 months.

questions.stem: Under the old classification, ITP became chronic after how long?
questions.explanation: Old: acute 0–6 months, chronic ≥ 6 months. New: chronic ≥ 12 months. B: End of the new "newly diagnosed" period. C: The new definition. D: Not used. E: Not used.

questions.stem: About what share of ITP is primary?
questions.explanation: Primary ITP ~80%; the rest is secondary (SLE 5%, APS, CVID, CLL, Evans, ALPS, HIV, hepatitis C, H. pylori, vaccines, systemic infection). A: Too low. C: Too high. D: Too low. E: Too low.

questions.stem: A woman with ITP is found to have Helicobacter pylori infection. How is her ITP classified?
questions.explanation: Secondary ITP causes include H. pylori, SLE, APS, CVID, CLL, ALPS, HIV, hepatitis C, vaccines and systemic infection. A: Defined by duration. B: Needs autoimmune hemolysis or neutropenia. C: Defined by failed treatment. E: No drug given.

questions.stem: Besides increased destruction, which mechanism lowers the platelet count in ITP?

options.A: Pooling of platelets in the spleen
options.D: Lack of folate for DNA synthesis

questions.explanation: ITP: increased destruction (autoantibodies, macrophage phagocytosis, cytotoxic T cells) and decreased production (impaired megakaryocyte maturation). A: Not the mechanism shown. B: TTP and DIC. C: Not the mechanism shown. D: Megaloblastic anemia.

questions.stem: In ITP, which cells phagocytose antibody-coated platelets?
questions.explanation: Antibody-coated platelets are taken up by macrophages (APCs), which present platelet antigens (epitope spreading). A: Not shown. B: Not shown. D: Make the autoantibodies. E: Not shown.

questions.stem: In ITP, which T cells destroy platelets directly?
questions.explanation: Tc-cell (CD8)-mediated platelet destruction is one of the mechanisms; Th cells help B cells make autoantibodies. A: Help B cells. C: Not shown. D: Not shown. E: Not shown.

questions.stem: Which bleeding manifestation is very rare in childhood ITP?
questions.explanation: ITP: mucocutaneous bleeding (petechiae, purpura, gum bleeding, epistaxis, GI, hematuria, heavy menses). Lecturer's note: intracranial hemorrhage is very rare. B: The most typical sign. C: Common. D: Common. E: Common.

questions.stem: About what share of children with ITP report fatigue?
questions.explanation: Fatigue is seen in 22% of children with ITP, related to the disease and its treatment. A: Too low. B: Too high. C: Too high. D: Too low.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old has petechiae and a platelet count of 15 × 10⁹/L. Which finding should make you reconsider ITP?
questions.explanation: Reconsider the diagnosis with recurrent infections, eczema, bone pain, constitutional symptoms, family history, dysmorphic features, organomegaly, lymphadenopathy, other cytopenias or blasts. A: Typical of ITP. B: Typical mucocutaneous bleeding. C: Supports isolated thrombocytopenia. E: Supports ITP.

questions.stem: A child has petechiae and a platelet count of 20 × 10⁹/L. Which additional finding argues most against ITP?
questions.explanation: ITP is isolated thrombocytopenia. Concomitant anemia or neutropenia warrants broader evaluation (e.g. marrow failure, malignancy). A: Young platelets fit ITP. B: Fits isolated thrombocytopenia. D: Supports ITP. E: Mucocutaneous bleeding fits ITP.

questions.stem: Which history best fits ITP in a child?

options.A: Sudden bleeding in a well child

questions.explanation: Lecturer's note: ITP = sudden onset of mucocutaneous bleeding. A normal exam with isolated thrombocytopenia supports it. B: Factor deficiency. C: Inherited disorder. D: Malignancy. E: Reconsider ITP.

questions.stem: What is the goal of ITP treatment?
questions.explanation: Goal: achieve a platelet count associated with adequate hemostasis. The decision to treat rests on bleeding severity, not count alone. A: Not required. C: Not the goal. D: Not the goal. E: Not the goal.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old with new ITP has a platelet count of 25 × 10⁹/L and a few petechiae, with no mucosal bleeding. What is the best management?
questions.explanation: 2019 paradigm: observe mild ITP → short steroids when treatment is needed → TPO-RA if first-line therapy fails. Treatment is indicated in mucosal bleeding with platelets < 10 × 10⁹/L. A: Not needed for mild ITP. B: Not first line. D: Not first line. E: Not indicated.

questions.stem: An adult's ITP fails a short course of steroids and she needs further treatment. What is the next step in the 2019 paradigm?
questions.explanation: 2019 treatment paradigm: observe mild ITP → short steroids when treatment is needed → TPO-RA if first-line therapy fails. A: Short steroids only, then a TPO-RA. B: Not ITP treatment. C: Not the next step given. E: TTP.

questions.stem: Rituximab treats ITP by targeting which molecule?
questions.explanation: Novel ITP therapies: rituximab (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody) and thrombopoietin receptor agonists. A: Not the target. B: Not the target. C: T cells. D: CD40 ligand.

questions.stem: Each is a traditional ITP treatment EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Traditional: observation, steroids, IVIG, anti-D IG, splenectomy. Novel: rituximab, TPO receptor agonists. B: Traditional. C: Traditional. D: Traditional. E: Traditional.

questions.stem: A child with ITP has platelets of 30 × 10⁹/L and no bleeding; another has platelets of 30 × 10⁹/L and heavy gum bleeding. What mainly decides who is treated?
questions.explanation: The decision to treat is based on bleeding severity and not just the platelet count, plus family/patient preference, QoL and evidence of durable response. A: The same in both. B: Not the basis. D: Not the basis. E: Not the basis.

questions.stem: A man receiving heparin after hip surgery has his platelets fall from 250 to 90 × 10⁹/L on day 7, then develops a DVT. What is the mechanism?
questions.explanation: HIT: an immune reaction 5–15 days after heparin; IgG binds the platelet factor 4/heparin complex and platelets, activating them, lowering their count and raising thrombin generation. A: Not HIT. B: HIT is immune. C: Not this picture. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: A patient develops heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with a new thrombus. What is the treatment?
questions.explanation: Treatment: stop heparin and give a non-heparin anticoagulant. A: Not the treatment given. C: Still heparin. D: Not relevant. E: The clot needs treatment.

questions.stem: Besides lowering the platelet count, what do HIT antibodies do?
questions.explanation: The IgG–PF4/heparin complex activates platelets, causes thrombocytopenia and increases thrombin generation, leading to thrombosis. A: Not the effect. B: Not the effect. C: TTP. D: Not the effect.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man has had fever and chills for a day and is now comatose and hypotensive with diffuse ecchymoses. Hb, WBC and platelets are low; PT and aPTT are prolonged; CRP is high. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Lecturer's note: sepsis/infection with DIC. Sick appearance, fever, shock and purpura point to DIC. A: Does not explain the coagulopathy. C: Does not explain the picture. D: PT and aPTT would be normal. E: Not a new illness with shock.

questions.stem: In DIC, which process is abnormally activated inside the vessels together with coagulation?
questions.explanation: DIC: a systemic, life-threatening process in which coagulation and fibrinolysis are abnormally activated within the vasculature, causing thrombosis, bleeding and end-organ damage. B: Not the defining process. C: Not the defining process. D: Not the defining process. E: Not the defining process.

questions.stem: Each is a recognized trigger of DIC EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Triggers: sepsis, trauma, cancer, obstetric complications, severe transfusion reactions. A: A trigger. B: A trigger. D: A trigger. E: A trigger.

questions.stem: A septic patient has low platelets, a prolonged PT and schistocytes. Which other result fits DIC?
questions.explanation: DIC: low platelets, prolonged PT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, schistocytes. A: D-dimer is high. B: TTP. C: Immune hemolysis. E: Low fibrinogen prolongs it.

questions.stem: A woman with DIC after placental abruption is bleeding, with a fibrinogen of 0.6 g/L. Which product best replaces fibrinogen?
questions.explanation: Treat the cause; supportive care with platelets, plasma or cryoprecipitate (a plasma product rich in fibrinogen) for bleeding. A: Replaces platelets. B: Replaces red cells. C: Not a clotting product. D: Not the treatment.

questions.stem: What is rapidly spreading skin bleeding and necrosis in DIC called?
questions.explanation: DIC presents with fever, profuse bleeding, shock, multi-organ failure, thrombosis, and purpura fulminans (rapidly spreading skin bleeding and necrosis). B: Vasculitis. C: Loss of connective tissue. D: Not this finding. E: Scurvy.

questions.stem: What is the main treatment of DIC?
questions.explanation: Treat the cause; give platelets, plasma or cryoprecipitate for bleeding as supportive care. A: TTP. C: Not the treatment. D: Not the treatment. E: Not the treatment given.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman has confusion, fever, schistocytes and a platelet count of 15 × 10⁹/L. PT and aPTT are normal. ADAMTS13 activity is 4%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: TTP: microscopic clots in small vessels, intravascular hemolysis and organ damage (kidney, heart, brain); ADAMTS13 < 10%; normal PT and aPTT. A: PT and aPTT prolonged. B: ADAMTS13 normal or mildly low. C: No schistocytes. E: No heparin exposure.

questions.stem: A woman with acquired TTP has antibodies against ADAMTS13. Which treatment removes them?
questions.explanation: TTP treatment: supportive care, plasmapheresis to reduce circulating antibodies against ADAMTS13, immunosuppressants, ADAMTS13 replacement. A: Not the treatment. B: Not the treatment given. D: Kidney support. E: Not relevant.

questions.stem: Why do platelet clots form in TTP?
questions.explanation: ADAMTS13 cleaves large vWF multimers into smaller units; when it is inhibited, large multimers persist and clots form in small vessels. A: DIC. B: HUS. C: HIT. D: Factor V Leiden.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old has had several episodes of TTP. Antibodies to ADAMTS13 are absent and its activity is very low. What is the cause?
questions.explanation: TTP triggers: anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibody (immune) or ADAMTS13 gene variants (congenital). B: Atypical HUS. C: Typical HUS. D: HIT. E: DIC.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old has bloody diarrhea, then pallor, platelets of 40 × 10⁹/L, schistocytes and a rising creatinine. PT and aPTT are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: HUS: triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury; typically children. A: ADAMTS13 < 10%; brain and heart. B: PT and aPTT prolonged. C: No hemolysis. E: Normal platelets.

questions.stem: What usually triggers hemolytic uremic syndrome in a child?
questions.explanation: About 90% of HUS follows infection with a Shiga toxin-producing bacterium: enterohemorrhagic E. coli or Shigella dysenteriae. A: TTP. B: Atypical HUS. C: DIC. D: HIT.

questions.stem: A child has HUS without diarrhea, and stool tests for Shiga toxin are negative. What is the likely mechanism?
questions.explanation: HUS triggers: Shiga toxin (STEC) or complement dysregulation (atypical HUS). A: TTP. B: HIT. D: DIC. E: Not a TMA.

questions.stem: How is typical hemolytic uremic syndrome treated?
questions.explanation: HUS: diagnosis based on the clinical scenario; treatment supportive. A: TTP. C: Not the treatment given. D: Not the treatment given. E: Not the treatment given.

questions.stem: A patient has schistocytes and a low platelet count. What should be assumed until proven otherwise?
questions.explanation: Schistocytes + thrombocytopenia = thrombotic microangiopathy until proven otherwise (DIC, TTP, HUS). A: No schistocytes in ITP. B: Spherocytes, not schistocytes. C: Not schistocytes. E: Not to be assumed.

questions.stem: Which laboratory feature best separates DIC from TTP and HUS?
questions.explanation: DIC: PT/aPTT prolonged, fibrinogen low. TTP and HUS: normal PT/aPTT. A: All three. B: All three. C: Hemolysis in all three. D: Hallmark of HUS.

questions.stem: Which organ involvement is the hallmark of TTP?
questions.explanation: Organ hallmark: DIC, bleeding and clotting with shock; TTP, brain, heart and fever; HUS, acute kidney injury. B: The kidney is the hallmark of HUS. C: Not a hallmark. D: Not a hallmark. E: Not a hallmark.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man has GI bleeding and lifelong nosebleeds that needed platelet and red cell transfusions. His platelet count, PT and aPTT are normal, and his platelets are of normal size. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Red flags: severe mucocutaneous bleeding, transfusion dependence, normal platelet count. Glanzmann thrombasthenia: normal count and size, absent GPIIb/IIIa. A: Low count, large platelets. B: Low count, large gray platelets. D: Low count. E: Prolonged aPTT; joint bleeds.

questions.stem: A patient's platelets lack GPIIb/IIIa. What do aggregation studies show?
questions.explanation: Glanzmann thrombasthenia: aggregation only with ristocetin. Bernard–Soulier: aggregation with all agonists except ristocetin. A: Bernard–Soulier syndrome. C: Gray platelet syndrome. D: Not with absent GPIIb/IIIa. E: Aspirin effect.

questions.stem: A boy has lifelong mucosal bleeding, platelets of 60 × 10⁹/L and giant platelets. His platelets do not aggregate with ristocetin. Which glycoprotein is missing?
questions.explanation: Bernard–Soulier syndrome: absent or decreased GPIb/IX/V (the vWF receptor), defective adhesion, low count, large platelets, aggregation with all agonists except ristocetin. B: Glanzmann thrombasthenia. C: Collagen receptor. D: Collagen receptor. E: Not the defect.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old has lifelong nosebleeds, platelets of 70 × 10⁹/L and large platelets. Aggregation with ADP and collagen is normal, but absent with ristocetin. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: BSS: AR, absent GPIb/IX/V, low count, large platelets, no aggregation with ristocetin. A: Normal count and size. B: Normal aggregation. C: Reduced response to collagen. D: Not a platelet disorder.

questions.stem: A child has mucocutaneous bleeding, splenomegaly and marrow fibrosis. Her platelets are few, large and gray. What do they lack?
questions.explanation: Gray platelet syndrome: AR; absent alpha granules and defective secretion; bleeding plus myelofibrosis and splenomegaly; low count; large gray platelets; reduced aggregation with collagen. A: Not the defect. B: Bernard–Soulier syndrome. D: Glanzmann thrombasthenia. E: Not the defect.

questions.stem: How are Glanzmann thrombasthenia, Bernard–Soulier syndrome and gray platelet syndrome inherited?
questions.explanation: All three are AR, with early-onset mucocutaneous bleeding. A: Not as given. B: Hemophilia. C: Not as given. E: Not as given.

questions.stem: A man on long-term dialysis bleeds from his gums. Platelet count, PT and aPTT are normal. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Platelet function disorders: mucocutaneous bleeding, usually normal count; mostly acquired (drugs; uremia, liver disease, autoimmune disease). A: Count is normal. C: Inherited, severe, from childhood. D: Prolongs the PT. E: Prolongs the aPTT.

questions.stem: Each drug can impair platelet function EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Drugs: aspirin, NSAIDs, penicillin, cephalosporins, anticonvulsants. Warfarin acts on vitamin K-dependent factors. A: Impairs platelet function. B: An NSAID; impairs platelet function. C: Impairs platelet function. E: Impair platelet function.

questions.stem: About how common are Glanzmann thrombasthenia and Bernard–Soulier syndrome?
questions.explanation: Platelet function disorders are rare bleeding disorders, a small share of congenital bleeding disorders; incidence approximately 1 in 1 million. A: Far too common. C: Too common. D: The frequency of vWD. E: Too common.

questions.stem: In a global survey of rare bleeding disorders, which was reported most often?
questions.explanation: Rare bleeding disorders: FVII 6,264, FXI 5,192, Glanzmann 2,179, FV 1,560, FX 1,427, FXIII 1,126, Bernard–Soulier 361. A: Second. B: Less common. D: Less common. E: Least of those shown.

questions.stem: A boy with severe mucocutaneous bleeding has a normal count but abnormal platelet function studies. Which test shows a missing platelet glycoprotein?
questions.explanation: Diagnosis: abnormal platelet function studies; decreased or absent platelet glycoproteins on flow cytometry; genetic testing in selected cases. B: Shows size, not glycoproteins. C: Factor inhibitor versus deficiency. D: Not the test. E: Fibrinogen to fibrin.

questions.stem: A man with Glanzmann thrombasthenia keeps bleeding despite platelet transfusions. What is the next treatment?
questions.explanation: Treatment is guided by bleeding severity: platelet transfusion, recombinant factor VII for platelet-refractory cases, supportive care. A: Factors are normal. B: Fibrinogen. C: Factors are normal. D: vWD.

questions.stem: A 15-month-old boy has a painful swollen left knee and a large forehead hematoma. His maternal uncle has a bleeding disorder. CBC, PT and smear are normal; the aPTT is prolonged. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Red flags: a male toddler with joint swelling and a large hematoma, a positive maternal family history, isolated prolongation of the aPTT. A: Mucocutaneous bleeding. B: Normal CBC. D: Prolonged PT. E: Normal aPTT.

questions.stem: A boy and his maternal uncle both have hemophilia. Which inheritance explains this?
questions.explanation: Inherited bleeding disorders: bleeding in males suggests sex-linked recessive diseases such as hemophilia. A: Would affect the father's side too. C: Passed father to son, not via the mother. D: Not hemophilia. E: Not inherited this way.

questions.stem: Which is an acquired disorder of secondary hemostasis?
questions.explanation: Acquired: drugs (warfarin, heparin, chemotherapy), vitamin K deficiency, DIC, inhibitors of coagulation, liver disease. Inherited: hemophilia, other factor deficiencies. A: Inherited. B: Inherited. C: Platelet disorder. E: Platelet disorder.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old girl bleeds after a tonsillectomy. She had delayed umbilical cord bleeding, poor wound healing and two miscarriages; her parents are first cousins. Platelets, PT, aPTT, thrombin time and smear are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Red flags: severe bleeding with a normal coagulation profile, delayed umbilical cord and post-surgical bleeding, poor wound healing, recurrent miscarriages. Diagnosis: factor XIII deficiency. B: Mild; no umbilical bleeding pattern. C: Mucocutaneous; no wound-healing defect. D: Prolonged PT. E: Prolonged aPTT if low VIII.

questions.stem: Besides factors II, VII, IX and X, vitamin K is needed to make which proteins?
questions.explanation: Vitamin K is needed for factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S. A: Not vitamin K dependent. B: Not vitamin K dependent. C: Not vitamin K dependent. D: Not vitamin K dependent.

questions.stem: Besides green leafy vegetables, what is a source of vitamin K?
questions.explanation: Vitamin K is fat soluble, found in green leafy vegetables and synthesized by colonic bacteria. A: The liver uses it; does not make it. C: Vitamin D. D: Not a source. E: Not given as a source.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old with celiac disease has bruising and a prolonged PT. What is the cause?
questions.explanation: Vitamin K deficiency causes: low intake (breast milk), poor absorption (celiac disease, cystic fibrosis), newborns, prolonged antibiotics, warfarin. A: Not suggested. B: Not suggested. C: Would prolong the aPTT. E: Normal PT.

questions.stem: A 6-week-old exclusively breastfed baby who did not receive vitamin K at birth has bruising and oozing. The PT is prolonged. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Vitamin K deficiency is most common in newborns (hemorrhagic disease of the newborn); breast milk is low in vitamin K; the late form can occur as late as 3 months. B: Normal PT. C: Normal PT. D: Normal PT. E: Normal PT.

questions.stem: An ICU patient on broad-spectrum antibiotics for three weeks develops a prolonged PT. What is the most likely cause?

options.E: Loss of vitamin K from gut bacteria

questions.explanation: Prolonged antibiotic intake reduces vitamin K made by colonic bacteria; the PT is prolonged first (isolated in the early stage), then the PTT. A: Not suggested. B: Would prolong the aPTT. C: Prolongs the aPTT. D: Not the mechanism given.

questions.stem: A jaundiced man has a prolonged PT that stays prolonged after intravenous vitamin K. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Vitamin K corrects the PT in vitamin K deficiency but not in liver failure. A: Vitamin K would correct it. B: Vitamin K would correct it. D: Vitamin K would correct it. E: Vitamin K would correct it.

questions.stem: A man with a prolonged PT may have liver failure or vitamin K deficiency. Which result points to liver failure?
questions.explanation: A low factor V points to liver failure, since factor V does not depend on vitamin K. A: Low in both. C: Low in both. D: Low in both. E: Low in both.

questions.stem: Which clotting factor is NOT reduced in cirrhosis?
questions.explanation: Liver cirrhosis lowers the synthesis of most coagulation factors except factor VIII. A: Reduced. B: Reduced. C: Reduced. D: Reduced.

questions.stem: A man with cirrhosis is actively bleeding. His PT and aPTT are prolonged. Which product replaces the clotting factors?
questions.explanation: Management of active bleeding in liver failure: fresh frozen plasma, which contains all the clotting factors. B: Mainly fibrinogen. C: Platelets. D: Does not correct liver failure. E: Not a clotting product.

questions.stem: A man with cirrhosis has thrombocytopenia. What is the mechanism?
questions.explanation: Portal hypertension → splenic enlargement → the spleen traps platelets → thrombocytopenia. A: Not the mechanism shown. B: TTP, HUS, DIC. C: Affects factors. E: Not suggested.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl has syncope, heavy periods, recurrent nosebleeds and a hemarthrosis. Her paternal aunt had an early hysterectomy for heavy bleeding. Hb is 5 g/dL; platelets and PT are normal; the aPTT is prolonged and corrects on mixing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Red flags: combined mucocutaneous and joint bleeding, heavy menstrual bleeding, early hysterectomy in an aunt, prolonged aPTT. Diagnosis: vWD. A: Unlikely in a girl with mucosal bleeding. B: Normal platelets. D: Normal aPTT. E: Normal aPTT.

questions.stem: Which is the most common congenital bleeding disorder?
questions.explanation: vWD is the most common congenital bleeding disorder, seen in about 1% of the population, males and females equally. B: Less common. C: Less common. D: Rare. E: Rare.

questions.stem: About what share of the population has von Willebrand disease?
questions.explanation: vWD affects about 1% of the population, males and females equally; most are asymptomatic and found through family history or preoperative screening. A: Too low. B: Too high. D: Too low. E: Too high.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl has had heavy periods since menarche and has iron deficiency. A pelvic ultrasound is normal. Which test is most appropriate next?
questions.explanation: Think of vWD in every adolescent girl with heavy periods, iron deficiency and no gynecologic cause. A: Not for this picture. B: Not indicated. C: Not the first thought. D: Not indicated.

questions.stem: Which type of von Willebrand disease is most common?
questions.explanation: Type 1: mild deficiency of vWF, 70–80% of cases, AD. A: 10–20%. B: About 5%. C: Rare and severe. E: Rare.

questions.stem: A child of consanguineous parents has severe mucosal bleeding and hemarthroses. vWF is undetectable and factor VIII is very low. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Type 3: marked deficiency of both vWF and FVIII, AR, severe mucocutaneous and hemophilia-like bleeding. A: vWF would be normal. C: Mild deficiency. D: vWF activity normal. E: Qualitative; sometimes low platelets.

questions.stem: What defines type 2 von Willebrand disease?

options.C: A marked lack of vWF and VIII

questions.explanation: Type 2: qualitative defects of vWF, 4 subtypes, 15–20% of cases, mostly AD. B: Type 1. C: Type 3. D: TTP. E: Not type 2.

questions.stem: A woman with von Willebrand disease has intermittent thrombocytopenia. Her vWF binds platelet GPIb too avidly. Which subtype is this?
questions.explanation: Type 2B (about 5%, AD): increased affinity of vWF for platelet GPIb, sometimes thrombocytopenia. A: Loss of large multimers. B: Low activity. C: Poor binding to factor VIII. D: Mild quantitative deficiency.

questions.stem: A woman has an isolated low factor VIII and normal vWF activity. Her vWF binds factor VIII poorly. Which subtype is this?
questions.explanation: Type 2N: rare, suspect in females with isolated FVIII deficiency; reduced binding of vWF to FVIII; normal vWF activity; AR; treated with DDAVP or FVIII concentrates. A: Low vWF activity. B: Increased GPIb binding. C: Low vWF activity. E: Absent vWF.

questions.stem: A patient with von Willebrand disease has low vWF activity because the high-molecular-weight multimers are missing. Which subtype is this?
questions.explanation: Type 2A (10–20% of vWD): low vWF activity due to loss of high-molecular-weight multimers; normal-to-low FVIII. A: Increased GPIb binding. B: Low activity with normal multimers. D: Poor factor VIII binding. E: Absent vWF.

questions.stem: A girl with type 1 von Willebrand disease needs a dental extraction. Which drug raises her own vWF level?
questions.explanation: Desmopressin (DDAVP) for types 1 and most type 2 promotes endothelial release of vWF and raises vWF/FVIII 2–5-fold. A: An antifibrinolytic. C: A bypassing agent. D: For heavy periods. E: Not relevant.

questions.stem: A girl with von Willebrand disease has repeated gum bleeding. Which add-on treatment targets mucosal bleeding?
questions.explanation: Antifibrinolytics are used for mucosal bleeding in vWD. A: Not relevant. B: Not routine in vWD. D: Not the treatment given. E: Not relevant.

questions.stem: A man with severe von Willebrand disease has developed inhibitors to infused vWF and is bleeding. Which treatment is used?
questions.explanation: Bypassing agents (rFVIIa, prothrombin complex concentrate) in severe cases and with inhibitors to infused vWF. A: Inhibitors block it. B: Not for severe cases with inhibitors. C: Not the treatment given. D: Not the treatment given.

questions.stem: Besides avoiding contact sports, which advice is part of supportive care in von Willebrand disease?
questions.explanation: Supportive: no contact sports, aspirin or NSAIDs; estrogen therapy or endometrial ablation for heavy menstrual bleeding. A: Iron deficiency is common. C: Used for heavy periods. D: Not advised. E: Not relevant.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old has purpura on the buttocks and legs, knee pain and abdominal pain. Platelets and clotting tests are normal. Which test is most important next?
questions.explanation: IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura): small-vessel immune complex disease with purpura on the buttocks and legs, arthritis, abdominal pain and nephritis; check the urine for blood and protein. B: Platelets are normal. C: Clotting is normal. D: Platelets are normal. E: Not indicated.

questions.stem: A man with alcohol use disorder has perifollicular bleeding, corkscrew hairs and swollen bleeding gums. Which deficiency is most likely?
questions.explanation: Scurvy: vitamin C deficiency, defective collagen; perifollicular bleeding, corkscrew hairs, swollen bleeding gums; dramatic response to vitamin C. A: Prolonged PT, no corkscrew hairs. B: Macrocytic anemia. C: Macrocytic anemia. E: Not this picture.

questions.stem: A teenager has hyperextensible skin, hypermobile joints, easy bruising and poor wound healing. What is the mechanism of the bleeding?
questions.explanation: Ehlers–Danlos syndrome: inherited collagen defect; hyperextensible skin, hypermobile joints, easy bruising, poor wound healing. A: Scurvy. B: IgA vasculitis. C: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia. D: Platelet disorder.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old has recurrent nosebleeds, small red spots on his lips and fingertips, and a lung arteriovenous malformation. His father had the same. What is the mechanism of his bleeding?
questions.explanation: HHT: abnormal vessel development; recurrent epistaxis, telangiectasia on lips and fingers, AVMs in lung, liver and brain, family history. A: Ehlers–Danlos syndrome. B: vWD; no vascular malformations. D: IgA vasculitis. E: Senile and steroid purpura.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old woman on long-term prednisone has flat purple patches on the backs of her hands and forearms. Platelets and clotting tests are normal. What is the best management?
questions.explanation: Senile and steroid purpura: loss of supporting connective tissue; flat purple patches on the forearms and hands; tests normal; reassurance. B: Scurvy. C: vWD. D: Platelets are normal. E: Not indicated.

questions.stem: Each feature should raise suspicion of a severe bleeding disorder EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Suspect a severe bleeding disorder with early onset, prolonged, recurrent or postoperative bleeding, need for PRBC and other blood products, positive family history. Bleeding from a single site in a well child suggests a local cause. A: Suspicious. C: Suspicious. D: Suspicious. E: Suspicious.

questions.stem: Which feature favors an inherited bleeding disorder?

options.A: Onset after starting a new drug

questions.explanation: Inherited bleeding disorders: presentation in infancy and early childhood, bleeding in males (sex-linked), previous postoperative bleeding, positive family history. A: Acquired. B: Acquired. C: Acquired (DIC). E: Often ITP.

questions.stem: A well-looking boy has repeated bleeding from the right nostril. The rest of the exam is normal. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Well looking, bleeding from a single site only: local cause (e.g. unilateral epistaxis). B: Petechiae expected. C: Usually several sites. D: Deep tissue or joint bleeding. E: Sick looking, organomegaly.

questions.stem: A sick-looking 5-year-old has petechiae, lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Sick looking with lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly: malignancy. Well child with petechiae: ITP. A: Well looking, normal exam. C: Joint and deep bleeding. D: Mucocutaneous bleeding. E: Umbilical and surgical bleeding.

questions.stem: On which cell surfaces does coagulation take place?
questions.explanation: Coagulation occurs on the surfaces of platelets and endothelial cells. A: Not red cells. B: Not neutrophils. C: Hepatocytes make factors. D: Not red cells.
